article.title: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: 6-Question Quiz & Type Guide
article.meta_description: Take a quick Fitzpatrick skin type test, learn what types I to VI mean, and see how the scale differs from skin tone and undertone for makeup and color.
article.h1: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: A 6-Question Quiz and Guide to Types I–VI
article.body_html:
A Fitzpatrick skin type test sorts you into one of six types (I to VI) based on your natural coloring and how your skin usually reacts to unprotected sun. The quick quiz below gives you a rough self-estimate in a couple of minutes, then explains what each type means and what it can't tell you. It is general education only, and it is not a way to pick makeup shades.

What the Fitzpatrick scale is (and what it isn't)

A six-type grouping based on how skin typically reacts to sun

The Fitzpatrick scale was developed in the 1970s by dermatologist Thomas Fitzpatrick. It groups people by their typical reaction to sun exposure, such as burning, tanning, or both. Type I burns most easily and tans least. Type VI has the most natural pigmentation and burns least readily. It is a broad grouping, so plenty of people sit between two types.

Why it is not the same as skin tone, undertone, or oily/dry skin type

People often mix these terms up, but they describe different things. Fitzpatrick type is about sun reaction. Skin tone (depth) is how light or deep your skin looks. Undertone is the cool, warm, neutral, or olive tint beneath the surface. Oily, dry, and combination describe texture and oil balance, which is a separate topic again.

A self-test is a rough estimate

A home quiz relies on your memory and your own judgment. Use your result as shared vocabulary and a conversation starter, not as a verdict.

Before you start: how to answer fairly

  • Think about skin that rarely sees the sun, such as the inner upper arm, not your face or hands.
  • Answer from your natural coloring. Ignore tans, self-tanner, and hair dye. If your hair is colored, think about what it was in childhood.
  • Go with your usual reaction, not your best or worst day. If you can't remember, pick the answer that fits most summers.

The Fitzpatrick skin type test: 6 quick questions

This is a simplified quiz made for orientation. It is loosely modeled on the original Fitzpatrick questionnaire, which uses different questions and scoring bands, so other versions online may look different. Note the points next to the answer that fits you best. Questions 1 to 4 are about natural coloring. Questions 5 and 6 are about sun reaction, which is what the scale is built on, so those two count double in the scoring step.

Question 1: Natural eye color

  • Very pale or icy blue, gray, or green: 0
  • Medium or deeper blue, gray, or green: 1
  • Hazel or light brown: 2
  • Dark brown: 3
  • Brownish black: 4

Question 2: Natural hair color

  • Red or very light blond: 0
  • Blond: 1
  • Dark blond or light brown: 2
  • Dark brown: 3
  • Black: 4

Question 3: Natural skin color in unexposed areas

  • Ivory or very pale: 0
  • Pale or fair: 1
  • Beige or light olive: 2
  • Medium brown or olive: 3
  • Dark brown or deeper: 4

Question 4: Freckling

  • Many freckles: 0
  • Several: 1
  • A few: 2
  • Very few: 3
  • None: 4

Question 5: What usually happens after sun exposure without protection

  • Always burns and peels: 0
  • Usually burns: 1
  • Sometimes a mild burn: 2
  • Rarely burns: 3
  • Almost never visibly burns: 4

Question 6: How easily you tan afterward

  • Never tans, only turns red: 0
  • Tans lightly and with difficulty: 1
  • Tans gradually to light brown: 2
  • Tans easily to medium brown: 3
  • Tans very easily to deep brown: 4

Add up your answers: Fitzpatrick types I–VI explained

How to score the quiz and match it to a type

Add your points for Questions 1 to 4. Then add your points for Questions 5 and 6 and double that sum. Your total will be between 0 and 32. Match it to this range:

  • 0–5: Type I
  • 6–10: Type II
  • 11–16: Type III
  • 17–21: Type IV
  • 22–26: Type V
  • 27–32: Type VI

These cutoffs are a simplification for a quick self-estimate, and the bands are not perfectly equal in width. Coloring questions can pull your total away from your real sun reaction. For example, someone with very dark eyes and hair but a moderate sun reaction may score a type higher than fits, and someone very pale with no freckles may score a type higher than their reaction suggests. If your total and your answers to Questions 5 and 6 disagree, trust Questions 5 and 6 first.

Types I and II: typically very fair to fair skin that tends to burn easily

Type I usually means very pale skin, often with light eyes, light or red hair, and freckles, that burns quickly and rarely tans. Type II is similar but may tan a little with time. Both usually react strongly and quickly to sun.

Types III and IV: typically medium to olive or light brown skin with a more mixed reaction

Type III often burns at first and then tans gradually. Type IV burns less often and tans more easily, and is common among people with olive or light brown skin. Reactions in these groups vary widely from person to person.

Types V and VI: typically brown to deeply pigmented skin that burns less readily

Type V usually has brown skin that rarely burns and tans easily. Type VI has deeply pigmented skin that almost never visibly burns. "Burns less readily" does not mean "unaffected by the sun," so sun protection still matters (more on that below).

If you land between two types

This is common, especially near a cutoff like 10 and 11. Read both descriptions and pick the one that matches your actual sun reactions. The scale is a coarse grouping, so treat the result as a range, not an exact label.

Fitzpatrick type vs skin tone vs undertone

A simple comparison

TermWhat it describesTypically used for
Fitzpatrick typeHow skin usually reacts to sun, in six groupsGeneral context and conversations about sun reaction
Skin tone (depth)How light or deep your skin looksFoundation depth, overall color contrast
UndertoneCool, warm, neutral, or olive tint beneath the surfaceChoosing flattering makeup and clothing colors

Why two people with the same Fitzpatrick type can need very different shades

Say two people both score as Type III. One has a golden, warm undertone and looks best in camel, olive green, and coral lipstick. The other has a cool, rosy undertone and looks better in navy, plum, and rose. The scale puts them in the same group but says nothing about those differences.

Where to go for skin tone and undertone

For makeup and color choices, work out your depth and undertone instead. Our guides on finding your skin tone depth and undertone and simple undertone tests walk through it step by step.

What your result is and isn't useful for

Useful as general context

Your type gives you shared language when you talk to a dermatologist, aesthetician, or anyone else who uses the scale. It can also prompt you to think about how your skin has reacted to sun in the past.

Not a way to pick a foundation shade or a lipstick color

The scale has only six groups, while foundation ranges have many more shades split by depth and undertone. Two people in the same Fitzpatrick type can sit at opposite ends of a brand's range. When you shop, swipe two or three close shades along the jawline and check them in natural daylight. The one that blends into your neck and face is the one to take home.

Why every skin type needs sun protection

No type is exempt. A higher type number does not mean you can skip sunscreen, because everyone benefits from sun protection.

Where an app can fit in (and where it can't)

A cosmetic overview for makeup and color choices

Once you're thinking about makeup, FitCheck: AI Outfit Planner (free on Google Play for Android) includes a live skin analysis that uses your camera to give an AI skin overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions. The app also offers live virtual makeup try-on, so you can preview looks such as lipstick on your own face. For makeup, face natural light, hold the camera at eye level, and avoid filters.

What it doesn't do

FitCheck does not determine a Fitzpatrick type or sun sensitivity. Its feedback is an AI opinion, a second opinion at best, so use it as a prompt for experimenting and trust your own eye and comfort in the end.

Not medical advice: when to see a dermatologist

This article and its quiz are cosmetic and educational, and AI feedback, including from any app, is not medical advice, so please see a dermatologist or doctor for any concerns about your skin. They can also advise on sun protection for your own situation, which is worth more than any general quiz result.

faqs.question: Is the Fitzpatrick scale accurate?
faqs.answer: It is a useful broad grouping, but it is not precise. It sorts people into just six categories, and many people fit between two. A home quiz depends on your own recollection, so treat the result as a rough estimate.

faqs.question: Can my Fitzpatrick type change?
faqs.answer: The scale is meant to describe your natural, typical sun reaction, not a temporary tan or a dye job. If your answers feel different from year to year, that usually reflects how fuzzy the groupings are. Treat your result as a range.

faqs.question: Is Fitzpatrick type the same as skin tone?
faqs.answer: No. Fitzpatrick type describes how skin typically reacts to sun, while skin tone describes how light or deep your skin looks, and undertone is the cool, warm, neutral, or olive tint beneath the surface. Two people with the same type can have quite different tones and undertones.

faqs.question: Does my Fitzpatrick type tell me which foundation to buy?
faqs.answer: Not really. Foundation shades are matched by depth and undertone, and six groups are too broad for that. Test a few close shades along your jawline in daylight instead.

faqs.question: Can I skip sunscreen with a higher Fitzpatrick type?
faqs.answer: No. People of every skin type benefit from sun protection, even if their skin burns less readily. Ask a doctor or dermatologist what is right for you.

faqs.question: Can an app tell me my Fitzpatrick type?
faqs.answer: FitCheck does not determine a Fitzpatrick type. Its live skin analysis gives a cosmetic overview with beauty suggestions to help with makeup and color ideas, and it should be treated as a second opinion.

review.notes:
The article meets the informational intent. It gives a usable quiz, scoring, type descriptions, and a clear comparison of Fitzpatrick type, skin tone and undertone. It states plainly that the quiz is not for choosing makeup shades. App claims match APP_FACTS: Android only, free, live skin analysis described as cosmetic, live makeup try-on, and photo tips. It explicitly says the app does not determine Fitzpatrick type, and it has no medical, accuracy, storage or privacy claims. The dermatologist referral and 'not medical advice' text are present.

Suggestions, none blocking:
(1) The 0-32 scoring with doubled sun-reaction questions and uneven bands is a home-made simplification, not the validated 10-question Fitzpatrick questionnaire. The article discloses this honestly. Consider also noting that the quiz is not clinically validated and that bands are approximate.
(2) The FAQ 'Can my Fitzpatrick type change?' answer is evasive, and its claim that year-to-year differences 'usually reflect fuzzy groupings' is unsupported. Say more directly that the scale describes typical natural sun reaction. Mention that tanning and burning can vary with age, medications or health, and refer readers to a clinician.
(3) The CTA 'put your skin tone and undertone to work' implies the app analyzes undertone, which APP_FACTS do not state. Reword it to focus on previewing makeup looks.
(4) The original scale had four types, with V and VI added later. The article could also mention that the scale is criticized for not capturing the range of darker skin tones, and that all skin types can develop skin cancer.
(5) The coral, camel and olive color examples are generic and should be hedged as examples, not rules.
